Make the distinction between these two threads explicit so future readers do not treat them as one combined change.", "today": "2028-01-01", "tool": "create_doc", "arguments": {"title": "Helio lifecycle design lineage — onboarding trigger and activation definition", "body": "Date: 2028-01-01

## Two separate design threads

These are related onboarding/measurement work, but they were not one combined change. The trigger experiment changed **when an email was sent**; the activation-definition review changed **how activation was measured**. They had different hypotheses, scopes, and success measures.

### 1. Onboarding email trigger — timing experiment

The existing “See how teams use Helio” email was scheduled for calendar day 7 after signup, regardless of activation state. That meant already-activated and still-cold users received the same message on the same schedule. A mid-segment churn read found 3.1% churn among users who activated before the touch versus 7.8% among those still pre-activation after day 7, motivating a timing test—not a redefinition of activation.

`EXP-2023-02-onboarding-trigger` tested replacing the literal day-7 send with an activation-based trigger (`lifecycle_onboarding_trigger_v2`), for mid-segment only. The hypothesis was at least a 2-point lift in week-1 retention. The test ran for two weeks with a target of 400; after a 2.9-point treatment lift (p=0.05; n=220 in the treatment arm), the team waited for a stabilization cohort rather than shipping on first significance. The trigger later reached 100% for mid-segment and growth tier; starter was out of scope.

### 2. Activation definition — measurement review

Separately, the team reviewed activation because v2’s “first integration + two logins within 14 days” used repeated login as a proxy and could miss legitimate accounts whose integration was connected and data was flowing but who did not repeatedly use the UI. The intended successor, activation definition v3, shifted toward product value: **first integration plus at least one in-product event within 14 days**. Definitions were versioned and retained, rather than overwriting historical classifications.

This was a measurement-semantics change, not an email-trigger experiment. It did not set the onboarding send schedule or establish that the new definition caused retention to improve.

## Lineage guardrail

Do not describe these as a single intervention or combine their readouts: the trigger test evaluated email timing against week-1 retention in mid-segment; the definition review addressed whether the activation event represented meaningful product use.
